text:
A choice between guns blazing and stealth is not "play however you want"
Most action adventure games these days tout the line "You can play it however you want", and then provide only two examples (paraphrasing): 'Go in guns blazing', or 'take a stealth approach.' And they don't provide any other examples, because there are no other. And while these choices are fine by themselves, calling it "anyway you want" is complete nonsense. Because in many a games nowadays these two choices are ubiquoutous, so by the mere fact that the devs are mentioning them is testament to the fact that they haven't thought of any alternatives.

Take MGS:V. Their gameplay video showed five ways to go about a mission where you have to eliminate (read: capture/kill) an enemy commander: Sneak in stealthily, go in guns blazing, attach a C4 to a car and blow it up from afar, have your buddy take the target out, or ride a helicopter in Apocalypse Now-style. That is variation worth mentioning. Or take something like Dishonored or Deus Ex; immersive sims can really say you can play it however you want. Stealth, action, manipulating enemies with powers, hacking, diplomacy, and any number of combinations. That is worth talking about.

So what I'm getting at here is: Having a choice between stealth and guns blazing is not anyway you want, and if a game doesn't have any alternatives than those, devs shouldn't say it. My two cents.

Too often on this subreddit I see people depressed that they aren't as interested in playing games as they used to be. There's no rule that you have to be playing games. If something is getting boring, do something else for a while.
There just seems to be so many people out there who think that their lives must revolve around playing video games. And that when they are bored or not enjoying playing a game, there must be something wrong.

Boredom is just your minds way of telling you that you should be doing something else. So, do something else. It's not really that difficult.

Take a break from gaming. How long should the break be? However long it takes for your brain to say "I want to play a game". Once you get the urge to play back, you'll know what was motivating you to play in the first place. Or, maybe the urge won't come back, in which case maybe you don't need video gaming as a regular part of your life [that's blasphemy to say here I know]

Playing through the Mad Max game made me appreciate something that i've never truly appreciated in videogames before: Beauty in emptiness
Not since Fallout 3 have i been so immersed into a world that's mostly just an empty, barren desert. But the way Mad Max deals with this desert, the way it handles the emptiness of it along with the very methodical placement of camps and objectives is something that i never expected would be pulled off this well in an otherwise really overlooked game (Like seriously, this game is the tits for real). Now, to be fair what also makes the desert beautiful is the graphics and the lore that comes with Max's world. There's just something beautiful to just stand on a tall rock or hill and look in a direction, just embracing the atmospheric, melancholic emptiness of what once was a big ocean, broken down ships serving as shelter and burning fires from the Warboys' camps in the distance. It is one of the rare open world games that i refuse to fast travel in because the game handles the desert so beautifully and atmospherically. The only game i can think of that even slightly matches this, and also manages to create that beauty in emptiness is the Fallout franchise, particularly Fallout 3

text:
Valve seriously need to start putting a foot down on indie shovelware/horrendous greenlight and early access games.
So, Goat Simulator - fun game. Not my personal cup of tea, but it has some pretty hilarious moments. It was pretty creative, and did something a bit different. It was very tongue-in-cheek towards the massive simulator game market which has seen a surge in international popularity in recent times, thanks to the Greenlight marketplace.

Now, don't get me wrong - I don't think Goat Simulator is actually a "joke game". It's a funny game, and it's far from AAA Quality; but I wouldn't call it a joke. Actual development time did go into it, and the devs are continuing to work on expanding its feature set, ala the Goat Simulator Online/MMO expansion.

However, in the rise of Goat Simulator, arrived with it the true "joke games"; and like all jokes, they get outrageously tiring when repeated non-stop for what seems like an infinitely expanding amount of time.

Currently, we've got a metric tonne of titles all living off the "x Simulator" joke, which are mostly Unity3D scenes pointed at a couple of prefabs; but by far, the worst I've seen so far is Grass Simulator, retailing at a cozy €9.99. There are currently 134 reviews (mostly negative) - the most unfortunate sign of that being that we can assume at least 134 copies of the game have sold (netting just over €1300); for a prefab scene that would have taken around 1-2 hours to build, at most.

The problem here is that we're currently in an avalanche of joke games, simply due to the fact that people will actually buy them - and for someone struggling with cash who possesses the Unity3D engine, why not dump an hour or two of your time into setting up a quick scene with a few prefabs, throw it on greenlight, and get your rent paid up for the next month? The end result is what Steam is now becoming; a marketplace edging ever closer to Google Play levels of spamware.

And here's the problem - it's us. The gaming community are voting these titles in, while talented developers and their titles need to sit out in obscurity due to the power of the popular vote. Steam used to be a platform that did the filtering for us; when it came to indie games, there was a vetting process that eliminated the horrorware that is "Grass Simulator" and its counterparts. The days of popular indie gaming being associated with masterpieces such as Super Meatboy, Braid, Bastion and the likes is rapidly leaving our shores; and the bar is being set at horrifically low levels for getting your product sold on the Steam Marketplace.

Unfortunately, it's unlikely that Valve would backtrack on their greenlight decision; as a gaming studio whose profits now seem to solely come from publishing, it would be financially a bad decision for them to go back towards a quality-over-quantity approach to gaming.

So, let's discuss - do you think anything can realistically be done to stop the Steam Marketplace from becoming the equivalent of Google Play for PC Gamers? Or are we as gamers, even in a position where we can demand such changes be made to suit our own preferences, or our personal standards in cases such as these?

With graphics technology reaching the point it has, games need to focus on the things that are lacking now.
So many games now seem to focus on how amazing it can look, how photo realistic the rocks look, etc. I feel like, honestly, graphics have reached such a high point that we should be putting that on the shelf for now and focusing on the things that are lacking in these modern games. Sure, I can see an accurate reflection of my players surroundings when I look into his eyeball, but when I shoot a wall the bullet mark magically fades after 5 seconds?

We've made games wide, its time to make them deep. Focus on the elements that others don't. Destructible environments, immersion based interactions such as debris interacting with puddles, and more. Focus on creating good AI that isn't as easily taken advantage of, or focus on how smoothly AI interacts with the world (looking at you Hitman 3. I love you but the robotic nature of your AI is at stark contrast with the insane level of detail put into the evirons.)

I think games should care less about visuals and more about actual game play depth. One example is a game I just recently played, Genesis Alpha One. A neat idea, a blend of FPS, rogue like, management sim, and building game. Problem was the lack of depth, the game quickly runs through what it has and makes no effort to innovate. The graphics are pretty good, but the game play suffers for it. No reason it couldn't have been a simpler game, graphically.

Sorry if this is ranty or doesn't make much sense, I'm pretty tired. But I hope the point came across.

text:
Is the "investigate area + follow the footprints" gameplay trope overdone? What are some alternatives?
I'm about 10 hours into Ghost of Tsushima, and most of it is excellent. The gorgeous world. The fluid combat. The "guiding wind" as a natural replacement for mini-maps and waypoints. But for me, precisely one thing has ground the game to a halt, interrupting the great stuff with a trope that feels years out of date:

"Find clues + follow the footprints!"

It's the classic sidequest formula. Lead player to Point A. Sidequest begins. Look around for clues (usually, a bit of blood, a broken window, a stray arrow, some trampled grass, etc.). Notice footprints. Press action button every 50 feet or so to (yet again) "observe" how the footprints continue along. Eventually come to Point B. Engage in combat. Return to Point A. Collect reward.

Open world games have been doing this for years. The Witcher 3 is among the most well-known examples. You'd use your Witcher senses to see the glowing footprints to nudge you along to the next point of interest. Horizon Zero Dawn had several sidequests exactly like this. Red Dead 2 did this, although to be fair, it was a bit more subtle in that title.

And now Ghost of Tsushima. Look: I get why open world games do this. It's a tried and true way to get your main character to narrate plot points ("There was a struggle! The blood is fresh!"), and it gives the devs an excuse to move players to the next spot. But to me, it was never all that interesting, and now, it's painfully tedious. In my mind, it also wastes the potential of these otherwise innovative worlds.

What could open world games do instead, now that they've beaten the "footpints" gimmick deep into the ground? One example can be found in the same game I'm critiquing: Ghost of Tsushima. For a handful of "Mythic Tales," the game gives you a hand-drawn map with physical landmarks to look out for. You then explore the world yourself, getting to know the topography, staying on alert for the key structures/mountain/rivers, and eventually, you triangulate the location.

This is excellent! It allows the player to continue to form a relationship with the world, rather than mindlessly following footprints. There's no need to click your mouse or hit R2 every 50 feet to reassure the game that yes, you're still following the same very obvious line. It hands the agency back to the player. (RDR2 also does this with some of the treasure hunting, which I thought was also well designed.)

Are you also tired of the footprint gimmick? How do you think games—especially open world games—could do sidequests like this better?

text:
Kingdom Come Deliverance is one of the best games I’ve played that I can’t recommend.
I’m playing the game on PS4 and I’m close to completion. Purchased the Royal Edition on sale and I have been quite satisfied with my purchase including all the DLC.

This game requires a lot of patience. It’s a game set in realism. Things that would take a few seconds in another RPG take much more time. And I Mean Time in Real Life.

Not to mention that the game is very poorly optimised for the PlayStation 4, with loading screens being extremely invasive. Loading from the Main Menu takes about 4min, 10 sec load screen to enter dialogue with characters, 10 sec load screen to open map etc.

This poor optimisation has made the game more tedious to say the least. Lock-picking is a nightmare on controller too. With a lot of practice it eventually clicks. But since this is their first game and this is quite clearly a game made for PC I’ll give Warhorse a pass.

Now getting to the game, to put it in laymen’s terms it’s a Bethesda RPG with Extra Steps and more meaningful player choice. The story takes a while to get going but when the pace picks up it’s very engaging. The story is taken seriously but you will have fun with the game as the tone is quite light hearted. Henry is an interesting character and it’s interesting to see his growth. The cast that surround him don’t slouch either.

This is definitely one of the most believable game worlds you can play in. The world is harsh and brutal. Combat is a touchy one. In my humble opinion this is probably one of the worst combat systems in an 3D Open World RPG. While they make a noble effort to capture realism. Instead the jankiness and video game cheese are put in the forefront.

When fighting multiple opponents the combat system completely fall apart. You can’t keep track of your targets and can be finished in seconds. While the 1v1 combat is better either your opponent is a parry god that you can never hit. Or a country bumpkin with no armour that goes down in 4 shots. Unfortunately the combat in Kingdom Come fails to be fun.

Despite all of this I’m having a lot of fun with the game. There is a huge amount of content here, I’ve been playing for about 100 hours and I still have a lot of content to finish. I’m having a good time with the game but I cannot easily recommend this title to anyone. The requires a huge amount of patience from the player to learn the world and to properly interact with its systems.

If you do ever pick up Kingdom Come ensure that you have played a few RPG games before. Even as an RPG veteran this game took a lot out of me. This game takes the RPG experience to the next level. You have to think when playing this game. If you are someone who’s tired of playing games that hold your hand throughout the entire experience this is the game for you.

8/10

Since the release of Cyberpunk 2077, one of the complaints i've been hearing online is "It's not an RPG game" which...confuses me beyond belief
Now granted, CDPR didn't help themselves by removing the word RPG from their marketing slogans ( which is a bit scummy all things considered) but the game is definitely an RPG. If you considered The Witcher 3 an RPG, then CP2077 is far more of an RPG than the Witcher 3 ever was. There's more choices in your playstyles, there's more choices in your character builds, there's more choices in coming up with a backstory to your character where as the Witcher 3 locked you onto Geralt's specific story (which isn't a bad thing by the way but certainly not an RPG thing), many side gigs have multiple ways you can approach your objective Deus Ex style, the Skills and perks are very well crafted if you want to move your character in a specific weapon style and so on.

A lot of people have also complained about the lack of choices to be made and yes, certain parts of the game are very linear in nature but, there are moments, many in fact in the game where your choices matter. Hell, not completing some of the optional side quests locks you out of endings, how is that lack of choices? And again, so did The Witcher 3, in fact that one was even more linear because Geralt was such an established character. Also, i can't believe i have to say this: lack of choices ≠ not and RPG game. Are Final Fantasy games not RPG's because you don't get to make choices? Hell, is the JRPG genre as a whole not RPG because you don't get to make choices in them and the games set you on a pre-set path. No, obviously

Now listen, i'm a huge RPG nerd. Literally the first game i ever played in my life was the original Wasteland on my shitty DOS computer back in 1991. I've been through all the old school champions: The original Fallouts, Planescape Torment (I still have the original packaging on my shelf) , Icewind Dale, Baldur's Gate etc. No modern day RPG has ever and i mean EVER come close to the amount of freedom that games like Planescape and Fallout 2 had. The closest to even come to them was New Vegas and even that fell short, just by a little bit. But you know what, New Vegas is still very much and RPG game, same way CP2077 is, same way the Witcher 3 is, same way the Mass Effect games are, same way Fallout 3 and to a certain extent Fallout 4 as well

Max Payne has made me realise i'm getting tired of games with collectibles, secrets and other completionist properties.
Both 1 and 2 are fantastic games which have aged really well. The mechanics, story and graphics all stood the test of time (the graphics maybe not so much but its definitely not an eye sore).

Progressing through the story feels so good, there are small pockets of areas to explore but only to the extent of finding some ammo/health - there are no real secret areas or anything to really collect.

Playing through the game, at no point do i feel bad for not properly exploring the area because the only thing that really progresses at any point in time is simply the game's story.

The only thing completing the game does is unlock further difficulty levels.

One big thing i've felt by not having things to collect is that it gives you a chance to really soak in the games atmosphere, characters and environments.

When i enter a room i don't think to myself 'i wonder what sort of secret items may be in this room', instead.... i just think less, because i'm way more absorbed into the game's story.

I can't think off the top of my head many other games like this (mainly because i've not encountered many) - maybe Order 1886 on PS4? That felt like a very story driven game, not sure if there are any collectables in that though.

text:
I miss when online games had less rules and allowed for creative mechanics and gameplay. Case in point: When I was the lone healer of Graal Online.
I used to play a game called Graal Online which I think is still around, but I played it back when it was still in its early stages.

I don't recall how many players were on at a time in this game but I wanna say it was about 50 or so.

In this game, there was a player list with "police" that I suppose were like the mods of the game. They could change things about characters and things like that.

In case you don't know, Graal is basically a multiplayer game that looks and plays an awful lot like Legend of Zelda: Link to the Past. Here's a screenshot. I'm trying to remember what the game was like since it's been such a long time, but people basically roamed around together fighting monsters and solving puzzles, I don't think there was PVP at the time...maybe there were PVP zones? I honestly don't remember. There was a bunch of different weapons and items and things. It was pretty cool. However, there were no "classes", and certainly no healers.

On a total whim, having a preference for playing healers, I had an idea. I messaged one of the "police" players and asked him if he could change my character so my damage value was negative (meaning I heal when hitting) and make it so I could hit players, essentially making my character a healer. He thought it was brilliant and did so immediately, even offering me a choice of "healer type" weapons. I chose a golden scepter-type sprite as my weapon, and I adorned my character in colors that made him look like a medic. You used to be able to customize the shield that your character had, and I had a red cross on mine.

I drew attention everywhere I went, and I was super popular. I would roam around with players as they traversed the game world and healed them as they took damage. However, being unable to damage enemies, they had the duty of protecting me. It was such a unique experience, and one that I don't know that I or anyone else will ever experience again. I don't actually know if anyone else ended up copying my idea, but I don't seem to recall that they did, at least not while I was playing.

These were the wild west days of MMOs, when admins and mods had power over the game world which allowed for flexible and creative gameplay. Not that games today are bad, quite the contrary, but I do miss this kind of experience in online games.

Just wondering if anyone else has experiences from the past like this to share, or perhaps there might even be games around today where this kind of experience is possible!

text:
900+ games finished...but at a terrible cost
My Journey to complete my Steam Backlog

About 20 months ago, I set off on a journey that a lot start, but very few are able to finish – Completing their Steam Backlog. The whole thing became an obsession for me. It consumed most if not all of my spare time. I started the challenge with just over 600 games in my library, but by the end, I had over 950+ games. Now I can say that I have played, finished (or to the best of the game type) every single one of them.

I have to say that this enormous task has drained my interest in gaming, and no doubt I will still play games, but never to this extent ever again. I will take a huge step back from gaming completely. Maybe an few hours a week. Over the past 18 months I had spent 8+ hours a day gaming just so I could finish this goal. While I am happy I have accomplished my goal, it has come with huge penalties which I will forever regret.

I have a very addictive nature, although I have never drunk, smoked, or done any drugs. My addiction takes forms in different ways. Gaming is my biggest one. My addition has stemmed back over a decade, probably all the way back since I was 10 or 11. I never had many friends, still don’t, I just forced myself to play games to escape from the world I live in.

My addictive nature has caused me to destroy parts of my life due to my addiction to gaming, my backlog. It has ruined my relationship with my partner. Even though she always said that she didn't mind me playing games, at the back of my mind I knew she did mind. While I still spent plenty of time with her, I probably didn't spend enough, and I was foolish enough to want to be at home for an extra hour playing a game. That was 1) Childish, 2) Very disrespectful.

While the relationship is basically over now. I still want to write this post as to show a way of me owning up to my shortcomings and regardless of whether I finished my quest or not, I would still have quit gaming very soon anyway because of the way it made me feel. Our relationship wasn’t perfect all things considered, maybe my addiction to gaming was one of the biggest flaws, but there were still many issues which needed to be worked on, but she was still the girl of my dreams and forever will be.

My addictive nature not only takes form in gaming, it does for work, but that is not frowned upon as much as this, and I know that people will raise their noses at the sight of this thread as they’ll think I am pathetic and just need to grow up. And they are right, I messed up big time and did not have my priorities straight.

Now when I think of playing a game, I cannot, the thought just makes me shudder. I don’t think I could play another game for a good few months now – and for that, I am glad. I need to work on myself, and to stop my addictive nature, not just for gaming, but for everything. My clingy attitude towards people and things, needs to stop, my constant worrying about stuff needs to stop, and most of all, I need to have a bit of confidence in myself, my constant trust issues need to stop.

So, for anyone thinking of taking up their own completing the backlog challenge, please, take it from someone that knows from first-hand experience, do it in the right way. Don’t screw up what you have because you have an addictive nature and do it all in consideration of others. I am fully expecting a flurry of flame and blame comments aimed at me from this, and I will accept them all on my chin, but this post is mainly for myself to try get some thoughts down on paper, and to show people that even the smallest thing can have the biggest effect on people’s lives like this.

What’s going to happen for me in the future? Like I said, I am going to take a massive step back from gaming. But I am going to build a friendship with my ex, and I am going to become the best friend that she fell in love with all over again and try and rebuild our relationship. I am also considering selling my gaming rig to help fund a house for when we/if we want to get a flat to rent. Right now, I feel the worst I have ever felt, I am so disappointed in myself that I let it come to this and I am going to look to get some professional help if I cannot get through it on my own.

I know this isn't typically gaming related since there is very few gaming points in here, if the mods disagree that this should be posted here I will remove or they can delete, no problem.

Edit - Thank you so much for all of your kind comments. I whole hardheartedly expected some flame and I actually appreciate their honest answers.

Edit 2 - Thank you for the gold!!! Not the most perfect post to get it on but hey!

Edit 3 - Thank you for the second lot of gold..this kind of blew up and did not expect to get so much attention :|

text:
Sometimes, it's OK for a game to be short
First of all: I'm thinking primarily of indie games as I'm writing this, but I guess the same can also be applied to the AA/AAA industry to some extent.

Coming from someone very interested in the no-name indie scene, I follow some YouTube channels focused on playing through games made by one person teams, gamejams or alphas (shoutout to AlphaBetaGamer). Most of these titles are short stories or experiences that can be finished in 5-15 minutes of playtime.

There's without fail a bunch of people in the comments asking for the dev to make a full version of their work. Maybe it is because they loved the concept and wanted it to be longer? Or they wanted more of it? No idea, but they want more of whatever they played/seen.

That said, quite some devs interact with their fans. Sometimes, they actually follow through said requests and eventually work on a full fledged and bigger version... which flops hard on release. Ive seen examples of brilliant "prototypes" which ended up fading into obscurity after the full version.

I wish more people realized that, sometimes, it's OK for games to be short. Maybe that 5 minute horror prototype works so well because it's short and self-contained - not every game has the necessary content that can be expanded into a multi-hour game. Unless they have a pretty solid concept or novel gameplay idea, chances are they'll just end up with a drawn out and boring experience.

I would even risk and say that's the reason the infamous "Ubisoft formula" became the staple of open world games - have a ton of simple activities and checkbox objectives for the sole purpose of making the game seem artificially longer than it is. Because you can water down your game into something that will keep players occupied for two or even three times more than before.

Still on AAA games, I'm pretty sure most people remember the Silent Hills Playable Teaser (P.T.) so fondly because it's short enough to deliver its content/suspense without overstaying its welcome. I can't possibly count the zillions of "PT clones" that have since popped up promising a full game in the same veins of PT and subsequently failing hard on release.

I like to use a cake as analogy: would you rather eat a giant cake made only of icing or a smaller one but that's delicious? Of course, you can absolutely have a wedding cake that's not only good but also big, but they're usually difficult/expensive to make right.

Also, I'm not going into the "price/hour of entertainment" metric because that's a whole different discussion altogether. I'm focusing strictly on the experience and "feel" of these games.

So, what do you think? Is the shift to longer games something inevitable in the gaming industry or there's still room for successful short games?

text:
Is Cyberpunk 2077 genuinely ambitious enough to allow for said ambition to be used as defense of criticism?
Often when people talk about the quality of Cyberpunk, there are some who will say that many of the game's issues can be explained away, or excused, by the ambitious nature of the game.

I've been thinking about this a bit recently. After watching a few videos about both the actual game and its development, you keep seeing people talking about the, again, ambitious nature of the game.

Which is why I'm asking this question here. Is it? Like, is it really ambitious? People often talk about how "a game like this has never been made before" and I suppose yes, it's for the most part fair to say that an RPG made in this way set almost entirely within a city is a fairly unique concept. But just because something is unique doesn't make it ambitious. And I just can't bring myself to believe that anything about the game is particularly ambitious.

Because the game is just The Witcher 3 in a city, yeah? Without being overly-reductive, I don't think it's unfair to say Cyberpunk 2077 is, by and large, Witcher 3 in a city. And the city is big, certainly, and pretty detailed for such a size too. But nothing about the game screams ambition, for me. It doesn't even really whisper ambition.

The story is fine. Telling a story about mortality, and fear of death, even for one living a violent life, and a death out of your control, is fine. I mean, Red Dead Redemption 2 just did that, and better, but that's fine. The gameplay is largely rooty-tooty-point-and-shooty. There's a little more going on here than just that obviously, you've got some hacking and some melee combat. The loot system is, IMO, the worst ever. I could make an entire post on why it's bad and what I believe would be a far, far better progression system but, y'know, for now, whatever. And the game looks pretty good. Unless you look at it funny, then it might just explode.

But outside of that, there's really nothing. Every other facet is half-baked, non-existent, or frankly just quite shit. I don't want this to be a big criticism post because that defeats the actual purpose of the post, but just to name a few: lame non-main side quests (sider quests?(the ones where you're just given a 7 second phone call, 3 paragraph email, and 12 guys to shoot)), lackluster civilian AI, literally non-existent driving AI, also non-existent police systems, crippling lack of variety in tasks.

I'm not even going to go on. The game just has very little going on except the shooting of the men in the masks and the funny hats. If this game had the interactivity of Yakuza, the diversions of Saints Row, the character interactions of Persona, the destruction of Red Faction, then yeah, I'd say it was ambitious. If even one of those things, then yeah. Big ambition.

But just having a large city that is mostly just a backdrop is not ambitious to me. But what about to you? I'd really like hear everyone's opinion on this.

text:
Why I Miss Forums, and Despise Discord
Back in the good old days, forums and IRC ran parallel with each other and had no reason to intersect. With the internet becoming bigger, more consolidated and commercialized than ever, people are finding ways to spend time on as few different sites as possible. Forums have closed in favor of cheaper-to-run Discord servers. This has led to a great exodus on over thirty years of early Internet history. I miss these forums because:


Search indexing. This is the biggest downside to Discord and other IRC chats, there are no archival properties outside of the ecosystem. Unless you meet the requirements to join and in some cases are pre-vetted, accessing information is extremely hard with Discord servers. It is not very convenient having to join several channels and servers just to find one item guide on the character you like to use. Forums index all this information to be easily searched by the web. This is what they were built for.


Synchronous vs asynchronous communication: Discord is very fast paced and does not necessarily reward quality posts and comments, but instead to get known by posting as much as possible. You cannot communicate on your own time like on a forum, you have to lurk all day and hope you get in the discussion within time.


Server politics and cliques: Even moreso than forums I found Discord servers to be pretty cliquey. There is always an "it" person or group who controls the flow and nuance of the conversations. Diversion from these popular groups, just like real life, can lead to alienation whereas forums had more of an egalitarian vibe. Moderators seem way more involved on Discord chats than forums, for better or worse. I have found most moderators on Discord servers to be insufferable, and so does half the internet.


Online dishibition/anonymity: On forums your content is archived forever until deleted, and your presence on the whole internet, not just one server, is affected by the posts you make. It is also harder to change your name on forums. The more permanent presence of forums and the content encourage longform and high quality content. Shitposters were generally shunned. People are a lot meaner and more willing to bully on Discord I have found. An innocuous question posted on a forum will get a vastly different response on Discord, people seem more arrogant and crass because of the crazy level of anonymity Discord offers. After all, why not call that user a rude name or bully a noob? No one will see it 3 hours later and even if they do, I can change my name and tag and repeat again. I have been laughed, bullied, and trolled out of too many Discords to count but forums are generally more accepting and I have never been kicked or banned off of one.


Game Chat Dead: This is more of a function of party chats killing game chat as a whole, but it is nearly impossible to make friends and build competent guilds nowadays through game chat. Everyone rather sit on party chat or discord with their established clique, and playing solo queue is a painful experience. It's almost a self fulfilling prophecy. less people use game chat for party chat, so the people who use game chat get bothered by the lack of mics so they don't use game chat either.


I really miss the forums, and basically every one I grew up on was shut down. I get companies have to save money but it is a shame going on a Discord board only to sift through trolls and bull to find one piece of content I needed. The forum had it all right there.

As a car nut, it drives me crazy when people trash GTA 4 driving physics.
They weren't perfect but they were WAY better than the arcade style physics that replaced them. Sure, you could argue that GTA 5's driving was more compatible with the kind of gameplay you find in the series - weaving in and out of traffic, slamming on the brakes, and making last minute turns.

But I hated the switch to arcade driving. All of the cars felt the same - capable of changing direction impossibly fast, like they were on rails. The faster cars simply had even more unrealistically good braking and handling.

I understand that my opinion is unpopular, but hear me out - I thought it was cool to have a little realism injected into GTA 4 when it came to the driving physics. Miss a turn? Too bad, you can't slam on the brakes and stop from 100 MPH in an instant. That's how real cars work. GTA 4's cars had weight to them, and I LOVED that. You could do what's called a "Scandinavian flick" - using the car's inertia to initiate a drift by turning one way, then the other quickly to break traction. In 5? No way. The wheels aren't going to slide much because those physics were nerfed to make weaving in between obstacles easier.

TL/DR - I miss the sense of weight cars had in GTA4. They were more realistic, and I liked the difficulty that added. Drifting was more authentic, braking/handling were more lifelike - you had to really think about driving, unlike the arcadey nonsense in GTA5 that everyone seems to prefer because it's easier...

Gun-fu might be shooting games' most underrated yet underserved genre (for a reason) After doing research on it and clearing some genre specific backlog of mine, I've come to the realisation that one of the most immersive and satisfying genres I've found in shooting games specifically derives when it combines two of my favourite elements: martial arts and close quarter gun-fights.

If we look at it from a pure gameplay development standpoint, it's kinda tricky because trying to hit the balance between the level of agency devs can give gamers while also trying to making the gameplay look "cool" is a very tough balance.

One recent game that sort of started this for me was Blackwood (which admittedly is still a work in progress) and the upcoming game Spine. The devs would have to face the extremely tough challenge of trying to make set pieces manoeuvrable so that the player doesn't feel like they're watching a cutscene or making it so overly complex that a very reserve few would actually be able to enjoy something like this.

Some older games I've been trying actually had decent implementation of this included F.E.A.R and Sleeping Dogs but if you look at Gun-fu as it's commonly described (based off of John Woo's films), we have other candidates including the Max Payne series (with bullet-time), acrobatic games such as Wet (an underrated game imo). Even Watch Dogs 2 and Legion played around with the concept with sometimes it working extremely well and other times just kinda falling flat.

I'm interested in the new unnamed John Wick game project and excited to see how they decide to implement this while knowing tbh that it's gonna be a tough balance.

Games should have a permanent tutorial mode available on the main menu for long-lost returning gamers.
EDIT: I'm happy to announce that my upcoming game, Tempus Invictus, will have a permanent "tutorial" on the front, in the form of a Glossary. You'll be able to review all the game modes, as well as re-learn the abilities, items, and enemies all at a moment's notice. Check out my profile for more information on the game.

There's nothing worse than jumping back into a game that you were quite far in, only to realize you've forgotten how to play, whether it's basic controls, item interactions, crafting, etc.

A game that has a permanent tutorial on the main menu is Vermintide 2, and I'm thankful for it (even if the game isn't too difficult to get back into).

What usually happens is that I have to start a new account, then sit through the infinite amount of cutscenes before I can start the tutorial. And if there was a specific thing I wanted to practice, I might have to run through the whole tutorial or first few missions before getting access.

The best option would be to have a limited sandbox mode where you can see tutorial tips and have access to everything. What do you think? Would that be a mostly-unused feature on games and not worth the developers' time?

EDIT: While we're at it, why not have a recap feature that catches you up on the story up until your saved checkpoint? TV shows will do it, so why not games?

EDIT 2: While we're still at it, why not have a completely skippable tutorial and separate it on the main menu? That way, you aren't forced to run through a tutorial if you start a new game.

text:
Is there a specific name for 'static' game design set ups?
I was thinking about how a lot of games, particularly ones that come form the 2000-2010's era of gaming, have become lite-RPG-ized in their design. What I mean by this is like in the most recent example of Gears of War Eday.

In the classic Gears games, you basically had a set amount of abilities, and your character didn't really improve those abilities. Which is to say, you start out with a lancer, a gnasher, a snub, and the typical assortment of character abilities (melee, roady run, evade roll, etc). There were no levels, mods, or extra abilities you got intrinsically, the most you got to expand your combat abilities is whatever a level offered, like new guns or a turret section, etc.

In Gears Eday, you have mods that you unlock as you go through the game. You got passive armor mods, you got an ultimate ability, and you got 3 mods slots for all your weapons. This is to say, in classic Gears, your lancer was as powerful at the end of the game as it was at the starat of the game, but in Eday, you could give it a different set of abilities by the end.

This is a trend I've noticed with a number of genres though. Classic Halo also had a static set of abilities, but Halo Infinite has you picking various abilities and stat enhancements. Classic God of War games had levels to their weapons/magic, but the new GoW games are straight up lite-action RPG's. Uncharted is a less conventional example, but even there, you get a pike that helps you climb things about halfway through the game, where classic Uncharteds you had the same static climbing abilties the whole game.

So, is there a specific term for this old school type of game design that seems like devs have abandoned, where the abilities you have as a player are static throughout the whole game, compared to modern design that seems to take progression/customization of your abilities as a given?
label: analysis

text:
I think RPGs would benefit from scaling down their main story
The thought hit me while playing Hades - it's not even part of a genre that's supposed to care about its story, and yet I enjoyed that game's story more than almost every RPG I've played. There are many reasons for it - the writing is clearly better than what we're used to seeing for instance - but I think one key aspect is that despite being about literal Gods and Goddesses, the story feels very close to us and is definitely driven by the characters themselves. Because it's a smaller scale story about a more "real" story, it also gives room to its characters to grow - including the villains, which is much harder to do when said villains' goal is to literally enslave or kill everyone.

For instance I was checking out Baldur's Gate 3's description on Steam and the first sentence mentions the lure of absolute power. So I can already imagine a story similar to DOS2 with some world-threatening power that you have to beat at the end. I'm not saying the story will be bad necessarily (I don't intend to play until the final release in any case) but it's so tiring to basically always see the same damn thing, just reskinned and sometimes a bit more or less grimdark, but always with the same tone and themes. For similar reasons, I'm one of the (few, I think) people who prefered The Witcher 2's story over the third one - because it was much more "grounded" as you mostly fought for yourself and Temeria/the Northern Kingdom, not the entire damn world. And your ennemies were so much more interesting than the angsty Space Elves that the Wild Hunt ended up being. The best story in that game was the Bloody Baron's arc for me, and that part was definitely a lot more relatable than the end.

I get it, most RPGs are set in a classic Heroic Fantasy universe and it's supposed to be an epic story. But I honestly think that it's perfectly possible to create a story that feels epic and satisfies the player's power fantasy without having to be about a world-spanning threat.

Thougths?

text:
Games should make you want to stay and sleep at lodgings/inns/hotels regardless of in-game boosts
As somebody who enjoys immersive games, I believe that lodgings/inns/hotels should make you want to stay and sleep irrespective of any in-game benefits. Key features I can think of include the concept of "checking" into your rooms (not having to sleep immediately), having a few side activities in the lodgings (such as buying food/drinks, gossiping, playing games, etc.), and animations of going into the bed when you choose to sleep. Having lodgings with these features feels better to me than immediately "teleporting to sleep" after speaking to the front desk.

I also enjoy seeing lodgings that seem like lived in experiences; this includes creating enough beds/rooms to accommodate other travelers besides yourself/party, while seeing NPCs enjoy the side activities but also actually sleeping when the time comes. Skyrim does quite a few of these features pretty well that I often have not seen other games I’ve played doing so.

I’d be especially interested to see how to implement a more realistic hotel system for open world games set in the present day with current technology available. Sims 2 Bon Voyage hotels were able to introduce many features in their hotels such as restaurants, room service, checking in/out, and any other activities that the builder saw fit. Adopting such features for an open world game like GTA or a modern Final Fantasy game (if Square Enix ever wants to adopt themes from XV again) would be interesting.

I’m hopeful with the current generation of open world games/rpgs that the motivation/technology will keep increasing to better simulate nice hotel experiences, austere (or even shady) lodgings, and everything else in between. That would make it feel worthwhile to sleep after a hard day of roaming around/adventuring regardless of in-game boosts.

text:
Are a lot of indie games just glorified online flash games?
I understand that indie doesn't refer to a type of game, but typically indie games have lower production values. Much, much lower production values, to the point where just about every 2D game can easily be identified as indie. Now that doesn't mean they're necessarily worse, but a lot of times you see hype for indie games equivalent to AAA titles. I went on GameSpot and saw an announcement about an indie game coming to XBLA, as if it were any other game being released by a major publisher. A couple days ago there was an AMA from the dev for Gunpoint, and people were raving about how it was such a great game and they'd be sure to buy a copy to support him.

After watching the gameplay, I can honestly say it seems no different from a flash game from the good ol' golden age of flash games about 10 years ago, when Shockwave was huge, and school kids would go to computer labs to get onto addictinggames. The difference is, one costs typically $10-$20 per copy, and the other was free (for the player). One is reviewed in gaming magazines and websites and the other gets a 1-5 star rating from users. One is constantly hailed on reddit and by gaming communities while the other is thrown aside as being casual.

Look at a game like Limbo. The graphics can be recreated in flash. The length is the same as a lot of flash games (2-3 hours for the memorable ones). It's not a particularly super innovative concept. Sure the art style is nice, but style is independent of budget. And yet Limbo sold millions and was highly praised as being super artistic and worth ever dime. So what is it that makes indie games seem like the new direction of video games, while flash games have been tossed aside as cheap casual entertainment to pass the time here and there and never taken seriously?

EDIT: For the record, I own several indie games including Bastion, Meat Boy, Machinarium etc. Please keep the discussion focused on indie vs flash games, not on trying to convince me that indie games are good

Are We Ruining Games by Playing Too Efficiently?
I’ve noticed a weird trend in modern gaming: we’re obsessed with "optimal" playstyles, min-maxing, and efficiency. But does this actually make games less fun?

Take open-world RPGs, for example. Instead of naturally exploring the world, many of us pull up guides and follow the fastest XP farm, best weapon routes, or meta builds. Instead of role-playing, we treat every choice as a math problem. The same happens in multiplayer—if you’re not using the top-tier loadout, you’re at a disadvantage.

I get it, winning and optimizing feels good. But at what cost? Are we speedrunning the experience instead of actually enjoying it? Would gaming be more fun if we all just played worse on purpose?

Is this just how gaming has evolved, or are we killing our own enjoyment?

text:
I really love how the Avatar fighting game *mechanically* rewards you for roleplaying as the character you play
The Avatar Legends fighting game had its (seemingly) final beta this past weekend and while the game was already kinda surprising me with its mechanics and qol features, the thing that gave me the most fun was the "critical hit" system.

The basic gist is that every character, on top of all their general tools, has unique secondary objectives they can try to meet in the match and get rewarded for with advantages in-game if they succeed. Technically this isn't a new invention, recent MK games had a similar system called Krushing Blows, but Avatar takes the step of more deliberately trying to make these secondary objectives feel in line with actually embodying character traits and habits on a more personal level.

Azula, for instance, is a notorious perfectionist, and you're heavily encouraged to lean into that while playing her by pressing an attack button again at *just* the right time during some of her attacks to juice them up for bigger combos... assuming you haven't lost a round. Because Azula is a perfectionist if she loses any one round she transitions into her more insane Firelord personality from the end of the series and as a result she **has no perfect timing opportunities on her moves anymore**, instead you start the round with some extra power, less evasive movement options, and much more straightforward attacks for bigger damage and less subtlety.

Meanwhile if you play Korra, you're incentivized to be (as kindly as I can put it), a bit silly and reckless. The "Fearless" critical hit rewards you for doing, quite literally, running up to someone's face and hitting them with your DP, which if you don't play fighting games is basically just straight high risk low reward gambling even though it's extremely funny if it works. She's also rewarded, uniquely, for being the first person to land a hit when the round starts and, more importantly, landing bending attacks in the order of her Avatar cycle.

Hell sometimes the critical hits are relatively simple and just cute character quirks. The game has a pseudo-parry/dodge mechanic where if you start mediating, and someone attacks you, your character will do some cool little dodges and potentially punish the opponent. But since Aang is a pacifist, you get rewarded for using this mechanic dodge moves several times *but not* attack with a punish after. Meanwhile if you play Toph, and just hold down the button, instead of mediating she gives a character specific insult and takes some of their meter while giving her some instead, but only if you get the full taunt off lol.

There's way more than just these little ones, even among the characters I already mentioned, but I just wanted to appreciate out loud the surprising amount of depth that went into not just the actual fighting but also the character details itself. All this for a sprite-based $30 game in 2026 genuinely felt too good to be true, even if you don't like fighting games I hope anyone else who likes Avatar picks it up later this month, you'll have a lotta fun with it.
